title: Jeremiah 49:28–33
context: The LORD speaks through Jeremiah concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor, which the heading says Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck. Kedar is an Arabian people descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:13), known for tents and flocks (compare Psalm 120:5; Isaiah 21:16–17). The Hazor named here is commonly thought to be a region or group of settlements in the Arabian desert rather than the city in northern Israel, though its location is uncertain. The LORD summons an attacker to go up against the children of the east, take their tents, flocks, and camels, and cry terror on every side, a phrase Jeremiah uses elsewhere (6:25; 20:10). Nebuchadnezzar is named as the one who has planned against Hazor. The people are described as a nation at ease, living without gates or bars, and as those who cut the corners of their beards (compare 9:26; 25:23). Their land will become a dwelling for jackals. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage soberly, as shared ground about God’s rule over even remote peoples and the danger of careless security.

verses.text: Of Kedar, and of the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck, The LORD says: “Arise, go up to Kedar, and destroy the children of the east.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD summoning an attacker against Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor, which the heading says Nebuchadnezzar struck. God’s rule reaches the desert peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God directing even Nebuchadnezzar’s campaigns. Both traditions commonly read the verse in its historical frame without adding details beyond the text.

verses.text: They will take their tents and their flocks. they will carry away for themselves their curtains, all their vessels, and their camels; and they will cry to them, ‘Terror on every side!’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see tents, flocks, curtains, vessels, and camels taken, and the cry of terror on every side. Their whole way of life is threatened.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jeremiah’s familiar phrase terror on every side (compare 6:25; 20:10). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly.

verses.text: Flee! Wander far off! Dwell in the depths, you inhabitants of Hazor,” says the LORD; “for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has taken counsel against you, and has conceived a purpose against you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the inhabitants of Hazor told to flee and hide, for Nebuchadnezzar has planned against them. The danger is real.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see human plans unfolding under God’s purpose. Both traditions commonly read the verse within its setting, holding the location of this Hazor with care.

verses.text: Arise! Go up to a nation that is at ease, that dwells without care,” says the LORD; “that has neither gates nor bars, that dwells alone.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD calling the attacker against a nation at ease, living alone without gates or bars. Careless security is no defense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the danger of trusting isolation and distance. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against complacency.

verses.text: Their camels will be a booty, and the multitude of their livestock a plunder. I will scatter to all winds those who have the corners of their beards cut off; and I will bring their calamity from every side of them,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying their camels and livestock will be taken and those with cut beards scattered to every wind. The loss is complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God bringing calamity from every side (compare 25:23). Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, in its historical frame.

verses.text: Hazor will be a dwelling place of jackals, a desolation forever. No man will dwell there, neither will any son of man live therein.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hazor becoming a dwelling for jackals and a lasting desolation. No one will settle or make a home there again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see language also used of other judged places (compare 49:18). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober statement of desolation.
